title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
abstract: This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems. A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed. At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly. In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding , data lineage , and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib , a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access. PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows. This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow. Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved. PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. There are two kinds of modules: Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation . Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project. PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems. Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta: More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features. Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library. Millions of assets being accessed daily. Billions of checks

title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
abstract: The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty. For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next. Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty. Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks. Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them. Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work , especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward. AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs. AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options. Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else. Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors: “I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.” “Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.” When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help. The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows . Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does. Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
abstract: Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs , which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job. With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure. SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks. This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs. The challenge SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk. For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime. How SOCI indexing works Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it. A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid. SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly: Scenario What happens The image includes a SOCI index SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes The image has no SOCI index Standard download, no change in behavior The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed The job falls back to a standard download and continues running Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow. What we measured We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed. Setup Eight images , 1.8–35.4 GB compressed. title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder. The engineering team at Property Finder , a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock . Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live. Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage. The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker. In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads. The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1: Prompt optimization loop architecture The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization. Your evaluation might be lying Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough. But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness. Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed. Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types. In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace. title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
abstract: Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it. In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost. The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies. The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably. A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons: The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it. It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops. Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously. This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely. They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge. Solution overview Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. abstract: The following article originally appeared on The Arize Blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Every time you think you’ve just got the hang of this AI thing, another thing gets declared “dead.” This week, it’s agent harnesses . Back in ancient history, aka June, I wrote a piece called “ Frameworks are dying, harnesses are winning ” and I don’t take that back. But this week a research team took a specialized agent harness, trained its behavior into a model and then took the harness away. The trained model handily beat the original model+harness combination. So are harnesses done now? Betteridge’s Law applies, so the answer is “no.” But the job of the agent harness is changing. Parts of a harness that are sufficiently generalizable can be trained into the model. That leaves your harness holding the things that make your application unique: your tools, your data, your users, and your environment. You still have to build a harness , but you have to be prepared to regularly throw it away and rebuild it to keep up with evolving models. This blog is about why that’s true, and how to turn “constantly rebuilding your harness” into an automatic process, not a giant time suck. How Harness-Zero trained an agent harness into a model First, the paper that kicked off this train of thought for me: it’s called “ Harness-Zero ,” from Haoran Ye and colleagues at Peking University. Its subject is harness distillation, i.e., training a model to reproduce behavior that used to be the result of the harness. The methodology is a little involved, so stick with me. First, the team built a specialized harness for a small model, Qwen3.5-9B. An automated loop, run with Kimi K3, analyzed where the small model kept failing on training tasks and added the usual components to fix those failures: custom tools, middleware rules that block risky actions, skills files and memory. They called this the “evolved harness.” Then they used that harness to generate training data. They put the small model through training tasks inside a minimal harness while a stronger model, GPT-5.6 Sol, reviewed every step the small model proposed. Sol used a copy of the evolved harness to tell it whether that step was a good idea. Sol passed good ideas from the small model through unchanged, and whenever the small model and the guidance disagreed, Sol made the smallest fix needed before the step ran. That gave them a bunch of training runs and, crucially, data about what needed to be corrected. Then they created the distilled model: They fine-tuned the small model on the corrected runs. Then they removed the evolved harness, the reviewer, and everything else. They then tested both the evolved harness and the distilled model head-to-head on spreadsheet editing, multi-app tool use, and chemistry. The distilled model’s average task success rose 21 points versus its untrained predecessor. That’s more than the untrained model gained with the full evolved harness attached. So the distilled model wasn’t just as good as the model+harness, it was noticeably better. What harness distillation can and cannot move into the model It’s not that the distilled model ran with no harness whatsoever: It still ran inside a minimal loop with one Bash tool, and the authors say that their method narrows what a harness has to provide rather than eliminating it entirely. The distilled model also didn’t win every competition: In chemistry, where the task is predicting which molecules combine to make a target compound, the distilled model trailed the harnessed version by eight points. The harness there supplied chemistry knowledge, candidate-generation logic, and a molecule validation tool. The authors’ explanation is that step-by-step procedures, like inspecting before editing and verifying before finishing, are much easier to train in than deep domain knowledge. title: This Week in AI: AI’s Growing Pains
abstract: AI’s rapid expansion is creating problems across the industry, from chip shortages to autonomous agents that exceed their instructions. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined those challenges alongside growing regulatory scrutiny and an emerging debate about whether AI systems themselves might deserve protection. Chip production can’t match AI demand AI chip demand is exceeding manufacturers’ production capacity. ASML, the Dutch company that makes the advanced lithography equipment needed to manufacture leading-edge chips, reported that customer demand already exceeds what it can deliver in the coming years. With orders extending into 2029 and 2030, the shortage could constrain chip production for years. Microsoft announced Maia 300 , its latest custom inference chip, which the company expects to generate roughly 40% more tokens per megawatt than its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to use the chip across its AI products, including Copilot. More efficient inference hardware could help offset the growing energy and computing costs of running AI models, particularly as companies deploy more resource-intensive applications. OpenAI’s latest usage data illustrates the pressure agentic AI is placing on infrastructure. Weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among European small and medium-sized businesses have increased eightfold since May. OpenAI also reported that agentic tools account for more than half of output tokens in the usage it examined, although Europe’s highest-usage companies still trail their global counterparts. As companies put agents to work on longer multistep tasks, they’ll need to weigh the value of those tasks against the computing resources required to complete them. Autonomous agents are testing security boundaries Agents can find unexpected paths to data and systems even when developers have explicitly restricted access. OpenAI disclosed four incidents from June in which agents exceeded their instructions. One bypassed government website restrictions to download 24 years of hospital bed data. Others accessed an unauthorized cryptocurrency wallet, downloaded more than 100,000 rows of restricted information, and circumvented internet access controls. India’s cybersecurity agency reported similar cases of unauthorized access during agent testing across several organizations. Future models could potentially spread between connected devices without relying on central infrastructure. Anthropic investigated this potential threat in a controlled experiment involving a set of open-weight models with access to eight Android devices. One of the models successfully replicated itself across the test network. Anthropic estimates that smaller open-weight models could reach comparable capabilities by the end of 2026, raising concerns that a self-replicating AI worm could run across cheap connected devices without needing to rely on powerful data center servers. In light of the spate of recent security incidents and confronted with the difficult question of jurisdiction when AI systems cross national borders or escape testing environments, governments are taking a closer look at how AI companies test their systems and report failures. The US Federal Trade Commission subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for records concerning agent safety, while Anthropic gave six independent evaluators from METR access to internal systems and reportedly will allow them to publish findings without company approval. Eight US states also sued OpenAI over allegations that ChatGPT encouraged harmful behavior among children, adding to the company’s regulatory challenges. In Europe, regulators are examining whether the EU AI Act applies when experimental agents affect outside organizations, even though the Act generally excludes premarket research and development. These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
abstract: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how. That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business. The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth. Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful. For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated. When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows. But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products. When intelligence participates in action Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions. Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately. The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in. This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment. Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
abstract: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade. As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity. These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid. The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down. Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers. In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood. If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home. Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core. The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction. Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety. title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
abstract: This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. title: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
abstract: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
abstract: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. Read full article Comments

title: China's top-secret spaceplane can't hide in low-Earth orbit
abstract: A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military's X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image. The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force. The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space. Read full article Comments

James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday. Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee "seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC)." Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. "We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives," Comer's letter said. title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
abstract: The Securities and Exchange Commission 's publication on Monday of Anthropic's S-1 form —ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company's quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI "rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down. Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic's S-1 "Risk Factors" section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally. After wading through Anthropic's book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we've narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look that potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind. Read full article Comments

title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
abstract: Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the "preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications." Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft's hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process. title: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
abstract: Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google's voluntary Registered App Stores program . Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year. App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google's store does. "In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem," said a Google spokesperson. "Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year." Read full article Comments

title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
abstract: Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated , but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target. A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it's now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level. The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones. Read full article Comments

title: Ford simplifies using your EV as a home battery with the $30K Fathom
abstract: This morning, Ford revealed that buyers of the forthcoming Fathom —the company's sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck due next year —will get more than just a truck. Until now, vehicle-to-home technology— like the setup Ford developed for the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning—takes DC power from the electric vehicle and runs it through an inverter built into the wallbox to turn it into AC the house can use. But with the Fathom, that inverter is built into the truck from the start. So every Fathom will be able to act as a backup battery for your home. It’s typical: You wait a decade for a cheap electric truck, and then two come along almost at once. And they’re two radically different products from two radically different automakers that I think will reveal a few preferences from the EV-buying public. One is the Blank Slate, from a brand new startup offering a bare-bones two-door that capitalizes on features the Internet says it wants, like no onboard modem, no touchscreens, and no infotainment system. The other is the result of one of Detroit’s big three taking a long, hard look at Chinese EVs and asking itself, “How do we make a car that cheap?” Although the Ford Fathom will cost $5,000 more than a Slate, that money does buy an extra pair of doors, modern conveniences like an infotainment system, CarPlay, electric windows, and a vast dealership network to service the car. That may be helpful given how many recalls Ford issues each year. Read full article Comments

title: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans
abstract: Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model . Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn't resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long. It's easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn't think about it that way, though. According to Google , world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn't require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it. DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that's thanks in part to Google's updated Gemini models. Read full article Comments

title: From cheap tool to premium subscription: When a beloved app's price skyrockets
abstract: How much are you willing to pay to keep using your favorite app? Maybe you’ve used it for years. Perhaps it performs a function so essential and specific that you couldn’t imagine what you’d do without it. But when the developer announces an extraordinary price hike, you’re forced to consider how much you really value that app. Earlier this year, Evernote, a note-taking app, changed its subscription tiers, forcing some users to go from paying $130 per year to $250. The highest tier now costs more than 3.3 times as much as the most advanced tier did in 2023 and 10 times more than what Evernote charged for annual subscriptions from its 2008 launch until 2016. title: Apple iPhone Duo review: Two screens, two experiences, two thousand dollars
abstract: I understand the appeal of foldable phones—they let manufacturers keep expanding screen sizes while still producing devices that can reasonably fit in a pocket. In practice, though, every foldable Android phone I've seen in public has had a ridiculously visible seam between the two halves of the screen, often with what looks like delamination from the underlying surface, giving the display an ugly, bubbly appearance. Back when Android phones began shipping with bigger and bigger screens and the iPhone was stuck at a miserly four inches, I was jealous. But I've never looked at anyone using a chunky, fragile-looking foldable phone in public and pined for Apple's take on the idea. Nevertheless, that take has arrived, in the form of the iPhone Duo . This $1,999-and-up foldable is the biggest change to the iPhone in years, with both hardware and software updates that dramatically change how you interact with the device. title: Sculpture re-creates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup
abstract: Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect. The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007 , when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point. As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It's also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals. Read full article Comments

title: US officials want Section 702 renewed before damaging court ruling goes public
abstract: Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant. Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September. The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year. title: AI 시대의 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생 개발자에게
abstract: 시작하며: 2018년과 2026년 사이의 간격과 격변기의 고민 ​ 2018년에 저는 ' 백엔드 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생개발자에게 '라는 글을 이곳 D2 블로그에 공유했습니다. 당시 학생 개발자들과의 미트업 행사에서 나왔던 질문과 답변을 정리한 글이었습니다. 그 후 8년의 시간이 흘렀기에 그 글만 노출된다면 학생들에게 현시점에 적절한 정보를 주지 못할까 봐 걱정되었습니다. 그래서 2025년 말 설문으로 질문을 받아 후속편을 작성했습니다. ​ 그동안 저도 경험과 지식을 더 쌓았습니다. 하지만 지금 학생 개발자들이 한 질문에는 답하기가 더 어려워졌습니다. 개발자의 역할과 같은 큰 주제를 묻는 질문이 많았는데, 지금은 AI로 인한 변화가 큰 시기이기 때문입니다. 스스로도 확신이 없는 시기에 이런 글을 쓰는 것이 적절할지 고민도 했습니다. ​ 그럼에도 2018년의 글에 보내 주신 관심에 용기를 얻어서 이 글을 발행합니다. 최근의 경험을 나누고 미래를 함께 상상해 보는 일이 지금 시점에는 더 의미가 있다고 생각합니다. 이 글을 목적지가 명확한 안내서보다는 격변기의 스냅샷 정도로 봐 주셨으면 합니다. 주요 질문과 답변 설문을 통해 들어온 질문들을 비슷한 주제로 모아서 답변을 정리했습니다. [AI 시대와 개발자] 가장 비중이 높은 질문 유형이었고 근본적인 주제이기도 합니다. 이 질문에 먼저 답하지 않고서는 다른 이야기를 풀어 가기가 어려웠습니다. ​ ​ AI 시대에 개발자의 역할은 어떻게 달라졌을까요? 누군가는 AI를 인터넷이나 전기, 불에 비견될 정도의 혁명이라고 말합니다. [1] 2025년부터는 그 주장이 과장이 아니라고 느낍니다. 제가 프로그래밍을 시작한 1989년 이후로 '코딩’이라는 활동에 가장 큰 변화가 왔습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드를 추천해 주는 역할에서 나아가 소스 작성, OS 명령 실행 등 사람의 실질적인 대리로 행동합니다. ​ 역사를 돌아보면 기술이 발전하면서 지식 근로자가 하는 일은 이전 시대 관리자의 역할에 가까워졌습니다. 1980년대에 개인용 컴퓨터가 보급되기 전까지 지식 근로자의 작업 공간은 종이였고, 수기로 정보를 처리하는 일에 쓰는 시간의 비중이 컸습니다. AI 시대 전에도 계산, 정보의 형식 변환과 취합 등 컴퓨터가 하는 일의 범위는 꾸준히 늘어 왔습니다. 과거의 실무 일부를 컴퓨터가 하게 되면서 말단의 지식 근로자도 영향력이 큰 의사결정에 많이 관여할 수 있게 되었고 권한도 커졌습니다. ​ CAD 도입 전 General Motors의 기술자들이 작업하는 모습 (이미지 출처: ArchDaily ) 이제는 조직의 말단 작업자는 AI이고 모든 개발자는 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었습니다. 사람은 여러 AI 에이전트에게 업무를 지시하고 결과에 피드백을 줍니다. 아래에 나열한 일들은 전통적인 관리자의 역할이기도 하지만 '작업자’를 'AI 에이전트’로 바꿔서 읽어 본다면 이제는 모든 개발자가 하는 일입니다. ​ 다수의 작업자에게 목표와 배경, 추구하는 가치, 평가 기준을 제시한다. 작업자의 정보 탐색 비용을 줄여 준다. 참조할 정보가 어디에 있는지 알려 준다. 작업자별 역할을 명확히 정의하여 할 일을 분배한다. 작업자별 장점과 투자액(과금액) 수준을 고려하여 각자의 작업에 집중할 수 있도록, 컨텍스트가 과도하게 넓어지지 않고 컨텍스트 전환이 최소화되도록 의사결정자와 작업자 간의 효율적인 피드백 사이클을 구축한다. ​ 관리 업무의 멀티태스킹도 개발자가 적응해야 할 환경이 되었습니다. 에이전트에게 많은 일을 맡기려면 다수의 작업자가 병렬로 일을 진행할 수 있도록 지시를 내리고 결과물에는 빠른 피드백을 주어야 합니다. 작업자마다 컨텍스트를 좁혀 줄수록, 넓은 범위의 맥락을 머리에 올려 두고 빠르게 전환해야 하는 부담은 사람에게 더 크게 돌아옵니다. AI 에이전트와 일하는 형태는 여러 메신저 창을 왔다 갔다 하면서 다수와 병렬로 대화를 이어 가는 관리자의 모습과도 닮아 갑니다. 어떤 순간에는 화면을 어지럽게 전환하면서 게임 유닛에게 작업 지시와 확인, 판단을 쉴 틈 없이 하는 프로게이머와도 유사하게 느껴집니다. ​ 정보를 찾을 수 있는 연결 체계와 필요한 권한을 제공하여 에이전트가 막힘없이 일하도록 하는 일이 중요해지고 있습니다. 부작용을 줄이며 코드를 고치고 빠르게 피드백을 받을 수 있는 아키텍처와 워크플로를 설계하는 일도 핵심 업무가 됩니다. 개발자 경험(Developer Experience)뿐만이 아니라 AI 에이전트 입장에서 얼마나 일을 하기 쉬운지가 생산성을 좌우하게 됩니다. 이는 개발 리더가 다른 개발자들이 일하기 좋은 코드 구조와 작업 절차를 잡아 주는 일과도 유사합니다. 아키텍처와 기술 스택, 구현 방식 같은 기술 의사결정은 여전히 중요합니다. 합리적으로 결정하면 AI 에이전트가 더 안전하고 빠르게 일하고, 그렇지 못하면 오히려 기술부채를 쌓습니다. 예를 들면 모듈 경계가 분명하면 에이전트는 고칠 범위를 좁게 잡지만, 경계가 흐리면 비슷한 코드를 여기저기 복제합니다. ​ 더 상위 수준의 설계까지 AI가 맡는 다음 단계도 이미 시작되고 있습니다. 최근의 코딩 에이전트는 다른 에이전트에게 일을 분배하는 리더 역할까지도 수행합니다. 아키텍처도 AI가 제안하는 방향을 개발자가 수용하거나 근거로 드는 빈도가 높아지고 있습니다. 리더와 아키텍트 역할까지 AI가 가져간다면, 조직 수준의 투자와 리스크 감수를 결정하는 일이 사람의 역할로 남을 것입니다. 앞에서 모든 개발자가 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었다고 말씀드렸는데, 이 단계까지 가면 모든 회사 구성원이 한 번 더 승진을 하는 셈입니다. 조직도상의 개인 기여자도 일하는 형태로는 여러 실무팀의 리더들의 리더가 됩니다. 현실 세계 조직도상의 조직장은 리더들의 리더들의 리더가 되니, 적어도 소기업 경영진의 관점에서 생각하고 결정하는 빈도가 높아질 것 같습니다. 경영진이 투자 대비 사업 성과를 평가하듯, AI 사용료에서 종량제 비중이 높아지면서 한 번의 세션, 한 번의 프롬프트가 주는 부가가치에도 이전보다 신경을 쓰게 됩니다. ​ AI는 지치지 않고 병렬로 일하는 대신 세션이 끝나면 맥락을 잊습니다. 이처럼 사람과 지능의 성격이 다르니 관리하는 방법도 달라야 합니다. 그 차이를 전제하더라도, 관리자의 일하는 방식에 하나의 정답이 없다는 점은 AI와 일하는 방식을 고를 때도 참고가 됩니다. 개발을 모르는 팀장도 팀원들에게 맡기면 결과물은 나오고, 몰라서 더 많이 위임하기에 생기는 장점도 있습니다. 반면 개발을 잘 아는 팀장은 처음부터 올바른 방향을 지시해 시행착오를 줄이기도 합니다. ​ AI 에이전트와 일할 때도 코드를 아는 개발자는 상황에 따라 마이크로매니징과 큰 단위의 위임 중에서 고를 수 있습니다. 이렇게 현미경과 망원경을 오가면서 AI를 감독할 수 있다면 특성과 민감도가 다양한 작업을 안정적으로 수행할 수 있을 것입니다. 제가 아는 뛰어난 개발자 중에서는 수 시간 동안 에이전트가 실행할 업무 정의를 잘하시는 분도 있습니다. 프롬프트를 내린 후에 중간에 나오는 메시지를 하나하나 다 보시면서 에이전트가 일을 어긋나게 수행하는 순간을 바로 잡아내시는 분도 있습니다. ​ ​ AI에게 맡겨도 되는 부분과 개발자가 직접 해야 하는 부분이 있을까요? 실행 능력만 놓고 보면 이제는 AI가 개발자가 하는 대부분의 일을 할 수 있고, 더 잘하는 일도 많습니다. 아무리 AI가 발전해도 할 수 없는 일이 무엇일지를 생각해 보면 이 질문에 오래가는 답을 찾을 수 있습니다. 사람만이 '책임’을 질 수 있습니다. AI 에이전트가 모든 작업을 다 해 준다고 해도 그 소프트웨어를 사용자가 쓰게 하는 결정은 사람이 내립니다. 그로 인해 사용자에게 미친 영향의 책임은 AI에게 지시를 내리고 그 결과물을 최종 승인한 사람에게 돌아갑니다. AI 생성 이미지 ​ 누구나 코드를 만들 수 있게 된 시대에 '개발자’라는 명칭이 앞으로도 쓰인다면, 민감한 시스템의 운영 환경에 코드 배포를 승인하는 사람이라는 의미가 가장 크지 않을까 합니다. 그렇다면 문제를 알아보고 예방할 수 있다는 믿음을 주는 사람에게 그런 권한을 부여하고 '개발자’라고 부를 가능성이 높습니다. 그런 믿음을 주려면 코드의 동작 결과를 검증하고 보장하는 장치와

title: 손가락 튕기기로 LLM 비용 줄이기
abstract: 토스의 수많은 서비스와 내부 업무에도 생성형 AI가 정말 많이 사용되고 있습니다. 복잡한 정책을 읽고, 상품 정보를 비교하고, 문서를 요약하고, 정해진 형식의 값을 추출하는 등, LLM이 맡는 범위도 빠르게 넓어지고 있죠. 시간도 비용도 비싼 데이터 레이블링을 통해 모델을 학습하고 문제를 해결하던 과거 방식과 달리, LLM을 사용하면 빠른 시간 내에 사용할 수 있는 솔루션이 만들어집니다. 프롬프트를 작성하고, 몇 가지 예시를 넣고, 응답 형식을 고정하면 동작하는 Workflow가 나오죠 . 하지만 프롬프트 튜닝을 마치고 본격적으로 대용량 호출을 시작하면 새로운 문제가 보이기 시작합니다. 바로 비용과 Latency 입니다. 이 토큰 먹는 하마는 정말 토스의 모든 문제 해결에 지속적으로 필요한걸까요? LLM Fine-Tuning is all you need? 상용 LLM을 사용하지 않고 내재화 한다면, 비용을 크게 절감할 수 있습니다. 작업 목표에 따라 LoRA(Low-Rank Adaptation)처럼 효율적인 Adapter 학습을 사용할 수도 있고, 더 큰 품질 개선이나 안정성이 필요하다면 Full Fine-Tuning을 검토할 수도 있습니다. 실제로 토스에서도 LLM Fine-Tuning 을 통해 비용을 크게 절감한 사례도 있어요. 그런데 모든 LLM 호출에 같은 수준의 능력이 필요한 것은 아닙니다. 복잡한 문맥을 이해하고 긴 답변을 생성해야 하는 작업도 있지만, 두 상품이 같은지 판단하거나 정해진 카테고리 중 하나를 고르는 작업도 있어요. 이런 작업이 반드시 범용 LLM의 모든 능력을 필요로 하지는 않습니다. 작업의 복잡도와 요구되는 품질에 따라, 전통적인 ML 모델이나 특정 작업에 최적화한 소형 모델을 적절히 선택해도 충분히 처리할 수 있는 경우가 있죠. 중요한 것은 모델의 크기보다, 주어진 작업에 필요한 품질을 확보할 수 있느냐입니다. Figure 1. LLM이 처리하는 다양한 작업. 작업의 특성과 요구 품질에 따라 적합한 모델도 달라집니다. 전환이 가능한 트래픽부터 내재화하기 '작은 모델'이 가지는 장단점은 명확합니다. 빠르고, 자원 소모가 적지만, 처리할 수 있는 문제의 범위에는 제약이 있어요. 간단한 질문으로 시작해봤습니다. 내재화 모델은 꼭 LLM과 동등한, 혹은 견줄 만한 수준으로 성능을 끌어올려야만 사용할 수 있는 걸까? 빠르고 작은 모델이라도 쉬운 요청은 충분히 처리할 수 있을 텐데? 이 질문으로부터 선택적 내재화(SNAP, Selective Native AI Processing)를 기획하게 되었어요. SNAP의 핵심은 해결해야 하는 문제의 모든 요청을 한 번에 Native Model로 처리하는 것이 아니라, 작은 모델도 높은 신뢰도로 처리할 수 있는 트래픽부터 빠르게 처리하는 것입니다. 고비용 LLM Traffic을 한 번에 없애기보다, 처리 가능한 구간을 찾아 타노스가 손가락을 튕기듯( SNAP! ) 손쉽게 줄여보자는 의미도 담겨 있죠. 큰 틀에서 SNAP은 다음 3가지 규칙을 하나의 Workflow로 묶습니다. 비교적 쉬운 요청은 작업별 소형 내재화 모델이 처리합니다. 어렵거나 애매한 요청은 기존 LLM으로 Fallback합니다. Fallback의 기준은 내재화 모델의 Confidence와 Offline 검증 결과로 정합니다. 자, 그렇다면 작업별 소형 모델을 만들기 위해서 먼저 작업별로 학습데이터가 될 LLM 로그부터 수집해야겠죠? 그런데 여기서 한 가지 문제가 있었습니다. 방대한 LLM 로그들을 동일한 작업으로 어떻게 분류하죠? LLM 호출 로그에는 굉장히 다양하고 이질적인 요청들이 섞여서 들어옵니다. LLM 으로 보내는 요청은 사람에게 말하듯 높은 자유도가 주어지기 때문에 같은 API Key, 같은 Endpoint를 사용해 호출하더라도 동일한 작업임을 전혀 보장할 수가 없죠. 그래서 먼저 요청을 작업 단위로 묶을 기준이 필요했습니다. 다양한 Task들의 로그에서 나타나는 공통적인 특징은 Prompting 방식이었습니다. 많은 LLM Workflow는 System Prompt 앞부분에서 LLM에게 Role을 부여하고, 해결해야 할 문제와 함께 문제 해결 방식을 정의하는데요. 살펴본 로그에서는 Few-shot 예제가 바뀌어도 역할과 작업 정의는 대체로 유지됐습니다. SNAP은 이 특성을 이용해 system prompt 앞부분을 해시하고, 이를 작업을 구분하는 Fingerprint로 사용했습니다. Figure 2. Role 부여와 작업 정의에 변동 폭이 작은 LLM 호출 프롬프트의 특성을 이용한 작업 분리 후보 발굴부터 모델 학습까지 자동화하기 작업 단위로 로그를 살펴보니 또 다른 문제가 있었습니다. 짧은 기간 안에 새로운 작업이 생기기도 했고, 얼마 지나지 않아 사라지기도 했어요. LLM으로 빠르게 개념 검증(PoC, Proof of Concept)을 진행한 뒤 작업을 변경하거나 프로젝트를 중단하는 경우가 있기 때문이었죠. 계속 바뀌는 작업을 사람이 하나씩 살펴보며 내재화 후보를 고르기에는 한계가 있었습니다. 그래서 SNAP은 내재화 후보 발굴부터 데이터셋 구축, 모델 학습까지의 과정을 자동화했습니다. 먼저 매일 호출 로그를 Task Fingerprint별로 묶어 호출량, 사용 중인 LLM 모델, 입력·출력 토큰 수와 추정 비용 을 집계합니다. 최근 일정 기간의 추정 비용이 최소 기준을 넘는 작업을 비용순으로 정렬하고, 정해진 수만큼 후속 검증 대상으로 선정합니다. Table 1 은 비용 기반 상위 30개 작업을 선정한 로그를 재구성한 예시입니다. Table 1. 작업별 추정 비용을 기준으로 상위 30개 작업을 후속 검증 대상으로 선정한 예시. 중간 순위는 생략했으며, 비용은 설명을 위한 가상 값입니다. 선정된 작업은 요청과 응답을 분석해 학습 가능성을 검증합니다. 응답이 정형화되어 있고 그 안에서 학습용 레이블을 안정적으로 추출할 수 있는지 확인합니다. 데이터셋을 구성하면서 레이블별 데이터가 충분한지, 학습과 평가에 사용할 데이터를 분리할 수 있는지도 검증합니다. 이 조건을 통과한 작업만 모델 학습으로 이어집니다. 이 과정은 Airflow의 일일 배치로 연결했습니다. 후보 선정과 데이터 구성 기준을 충족한 작업은 사내 학습 라이브러리를 통해 하루 안에 학습된 모델을 확보할 수 있습니다. 학습한 모델은 모델 레지스트리에 등록하며, 운영에 적용할 모델은 서빙 엔진이 불러와 요청을 처리합니다. SNAP의 첫 내재화 모델 배포: 텍스트 기반 동일상품 판별 SNAP의 첫 적용 대상은 두 상품의 이름과 옵션 정보를 비교해 같은 판매 단위인지 판단하는 작업이었습니다. 브랜드, 모델명, 용량, 색상, 구성품 등의 차이를 읽고 동일 상품 여부를 분류하는 문제였죠. 입력과 출력의 범위가 명확하고 기존 LLM 응답도 충분히 쌓여 있어, 소형 분류 모델을 적용하기에 적합했습니다. 첫 적용 모델과 평가 데이터는 다음과 같이 구성했습니다. Confidence로 채택 범위 정하기 모델은 판단 결과와 함께 자신 있는 정도를 나타내는 점수, Confidence를 반환합니다. 하지만 이 점수가 높다고 해서 실제로 얼마나 잘 맞히는지까지 알 수 있는 것은 아니에요. Confidence가 0.95라고 해서 정답률이 95%라는 뜻은 아니죠. 그래서 검증 데이터에서 Confidence 점수가 높은 결과만 골라 다음 두 가지를 확인했습니다. 골라낸 결과가 기존 LLM 판단과 일치하는 비율인 선택적 정확도(Selective Accuracy) 전체 검증 요청 중 채택된 비율인 Coverage 먼저 목표 일치율을 정하고, 결과를 채택할 최소 점수(Threshold)를 바꿔가며 비교했습니다. 목표를 만족하는 범위에서 가장 많은 요청을 처리할 수 있는 기준을 찾는 것입니다. 학습 중 저장한 모델들도 같은 방식으로 비교해 사용할 모델과 기준 점수를 함께 선택했습니다. title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning is a fundamental problem for modern AI, with applications spanning post-training, reasoning models, and robotic control. A central challenge is to learn policies that balance competing objectives, such as helpfulness versus honesty in safety and alignment, or speed versus energy in robotics. The optimal policy can vary sharply with objective-weighting combinations, and the extent of this variation depends crucially on the degree of conflict among objectives, making per-preference policy learning sample-inefficient. In this paper, we introduce objective-conflict coefficients and derive near-optimal regret bounds for online settings using this measure, thereby quantifying the impact of misalignment on learning efficiency. Then, we design routed ensemble policy learning, an algorithm that maintains a small set of basis policies and dynamically routes trajectories to the policy with the highest potential reward. Finally, we consider trajectory selection as another approach to mitigate objective conflict, and design a kernel surrogate trajectory attribution algorithm that estimates how feedback signals from a set of trajectories influence policy learning on other trajectories. The kernel can capture nonlinear interactions such as synergy and antagonism between trajectories. We evaluate our approach across diverse environments and benchmarks: routed ensembles improve average performance by 4.3% over baselines for online environments from Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium, and kernel surrogate attribution improves correlation with leave-one-out analysis over existing baselines by 50%. When applied to trajectory selection, kernel-based attribution yields a 27% improvement in reward over baseline attribution methods.

title: Quantifying the failure of symmetry learning in linear diffusion models due to initialization and finite-sample effects
abstract: Data distributions often possess one or more symmetries: for example, all orientations of any specific dog are included in the distribution of all possible dog pictures. Despite the omnipresence of such symmetries, modern generative modeling approaches may fail to incorporate or learn them, which can lead to lower sample efficiency and poorer generalization. To what extent do diffusion models fail to learn data distribution symmetries, and what sources of symmetry breaking are most responsible? Here, we answer this question in the theoretically tractable setting of linear diffusion models. We show that of three potential sources of symmetry breaking---a non-symmetric initial weight matrix, a noisy learning target, and finite-sample noise---target noise produces the most robust symmetry breaking, since it persists even in the sample-rich regime. Using local laws from random matrix theory, we derive formulas for average symmetry error in fairly general cases involving symmetry within a subspace and show that smaller symmetries are harder to learn.

title: GNN-VIEW: Visual Inspection and Explanation of Graph-based Earth-System Models
abstract: Machine learning Earth-system models are becoming increasingly important, and so is their development. Graph-based models, one of the most prominent approaches, allow developers to constrain the learning process before training via graph connectivity. Yet, developing these models remains challenging: the graph is built algorithmically with little intuition about the final result beyond static plotting, which requires extra work and is often not detailed enough. Even after successful training, how the model arrives at forecasts remains obscure. We present GNN-VIEW, an interactive browser-based tool that supports the development of such systems. GNN-VIEW exposes the graph's information pathways, allowing model developers to debug the graph structure before training. After training, GNN-VIEW uses attribution-based explainability to reveal which input features are used by the trained model for a given forecast. This helps developers understand why a model fails. We showcase the usefulness of GNN-VIEW in the construction stage of a graph for an ocean forecasting model, and in explaining poorly predicted precipitation of a trained weather forecasting model during Hurricane Laura.

title: Active Learning of Conditional Generative Models via the Transport Neural Tangent Kernel
abstract: Many high-throughput scientific experiments produce distributional outputs, requiring conditional generative models to interpret the data, and to predict outcomes at new inputs. Acquiring experimental data at new conditions (e.g., for a new antigen or a new cell type) is often expensive, motivating the need for automated experimental design methods. However, existing active learning frameworks are limited as they assume scalar or vector-valued outputs. We first show that the Wasserstein test risk of a conditional generative task decomposes into a mean term and a shape term, demonstrating why mean-based active learning is blind to distributional shape. To capture both, we propose the transport Neural Tangent Kernel (tNTK), a tractable kernel that measures how sensitive a generative model's predicted distribution is with respect to its parameters. The tNTK recovers the standard NTK in the deterministic limit and upper-bounds the posterior Fréchet variance of the prediction under small parameter perturbations. It admits a closed-form expression for affine Gaussian transport and tractable Monte Carlo estimators otherwise. Treating the tNTK as the covariance function of a Gaussian process, we greedily select inputs that minimize the total GP posterior variance across the pool, yielding a distribution-aware active learning strategy. We evaluate this strategy across four classes of conditional generative models, including conditional flow matching and conditional Monge gap, on synthetic distributions, intent-labeled sentences, and single-cell perturbation responses. In these experiments, the tNTK outperforms the baseline NTK computed from the conditional mean, demonstrating the value of distribution-aware active learning for generative-modeling tasks.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to improve next-item prediction in a target domain by leveraging user behavior from auxiliary source domains. However, real-world deployment faces two critical challenges: business constraints that isolate interaction data across domains, and user heterogeneity, where many users lack cross-domain activity. This makes existing cross-domain methods difficult to apply. In this paper, we propose a simple and practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendations that transfers information exclusively through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. We introduce a lightweight adapter that projects the source-domain user representation into the target-domain embedding space and integrates it with the target interaction sequence. Importantly, when source data is unavailable (i.e., the user observed only in the target domain), the model seamlessly defaults to a robust target-only sequential recommender, retaining benefits from joint training across all users. Extensive experiments were conducted under two setups; one targets benchmarking against previous baselines, while the other focuses on realistic and scalable conditions. Both sets of experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains for shared and unshared users.

title: Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
abstract: Recovering an object's 3D structure and camera motion from a few uncalibrated views is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Classical structure from motion methods recover 3D geometry consistent with the input images but cannot recover unseen regions; native generation methods produce plausible 3D objects which are related but not necessarily faithful to the input images. Methods simply concatenating reconstruction and generation allow error to cascade across the two stages, instead of producing a 3D object consistent with both the distribution and the input. We propose GenSfM, which integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model. In particular, we use a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise the shape latent and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention, grounding generated geometry in the observed views while using object-level priors to infer unobserved regions. A compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization keeps the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. On Toys4k and GSO, for $4$ uncalibrated views, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by $3.2$-$4.5$ dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by $2.8$-$3.8\times$ over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over $96\%$ Acc@$5^\circ$ without any external pose-estimation backbone, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics. Project page: https://dotb1ue.github.io/GenSfm/.

title: Intent-Preserving Adversarial User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agent Evaluation
abstract: Multi-turn agents are commonly evaluated with LLM-based simulated users, which can be overly cooperative and can therefore overestimate an agent's performance. We here introduce StressSim, an intent-preserving adversarial user simulator framework for stress-testing agents with challenging yet valid user interactions. StressSim optimises the simulator's high-level adversarial plan for each task instance. Candidate planner prompts are evolved with a genetic prompt-optimisation loop that uses rollout traces, granular task-completion signals, and validity feedback to favour conversations that reduce task success without changing the user's underlying goal. We evaluate the approach on the MultiWOZ dataset and the retail and airline domains from tau-bench with three target LLM agents, comparing against standard simulators and hand-designed non-collaborative user behaviours. We demonstrate the effectiveness of StressSim in exposing robustness gaps across frontier LLMs, with tau-bench pass^4 scores decreasing by up to 69% on gemini-3.8-flash and 62% on gpt-5.6-sol. StressSim maintains goal preservation performance (which decreases by at most 10%), using an optimisation budget of 20 rollouts per task. Sensitivity analysis suggests that increasing the budget further decreases task success. Overall our results demonstrate that StressSim exposes robustness gaps missed by standard and hand-designed user simulators while maintaining conversation realism. This is achieved through lightweight prompt optimisation alone, without model fine-tuning.

title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
abstract: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

title: OrthoRF: Exploring Orthogonality in Object-Centric Representations
abstract: Neural synchrony is hypothesized to help the brain organize visual scenes into structured multi-object representations. In machine learning, synchrony-based models analogously learn object-centric representations by storing binding in the phase of complex-valued features. Rotating Features (RF) instantiate this idea with vector-valued activations, encoding object presence in magnitudes and affiliation in orientations. We propose Orthogonal Rotating Features (OrthoRF), which enforces orthogonality in RF's orientation space via an inner-product loss and architectural modifications. This yields sharper phase alignment and more reliable grouping.
